preamble: The diphthong [oi] becomes [ei] when its rounded back nucleus unrounds and fronts toward the following [i] offglide. In Old Latin, *oi (and *ai) in unstressed syllables had already merged into ei by historical times; this ei later became ī. The o-stem nominative plural therefore appears as -ei in inscriptions such as the Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus (186 BC), Classical -ī, and the dative/ablative plural -ois likewise became -eis, Classical -īs; an older -oe survives only in poploe 'peoples'.

examples.from: Proto-Italic o-stem nominative plural *-oi (cf. poploe 'peoples', in a late manuscript of an early song)
examples.to: Old Latin -ei: virei 'men', foideratei 'allied' (Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus) > Classical virī, foederātī
examples.note: In unstressed syllables *oi merged with ei, which then raised to ī. By 186 BC the spelling EI may already stand for a very close ē or ī.
The a-stem ending *-ais > -eis > -īs was remodelled on this o-stem ending.

sources: Weiss, M. (2009). Outline of the Historical and Comparative Grammar of Latin. Beech Stave Press. https://www.beechstave.com/
